Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-03 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Owen Brooks (Redwood SE), Lina Chen (Olivegrove CTO), Aaron Dubois (Olivegrove ML Eng), Priya Singh (Olivegrove Platform), Speaker 1 (Product)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to align on time-to-first-token, decide whether to use hosted PLG credits or scope a dedicated pilot, discuss security and network constraints.

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I can see folks are on. Quick roll call?
00:05 Lina: Hey Lina here.
00:06 Aaron: Aaron.
00:07 Priya: Priya.
00:08 Maya: Awesome. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, joining with Owen who is our solutions engineer. Goal today is to understand your constraints for getting Olivegrove to first token and which hosting mode makes sense.
00:20 Owen: Hi all, quick context from my side — we usually recommend starting hosted for speed and PLG credits, then bump to dedicated or private if you hit data residency or latency SLOs. But depends on the workload.
00:35 Lina: For us, two main things: time-to-market — we want a working API hooked into our ingestion pipeline within two weeks — and data controls. Some datasets are PII; we may need VPC or on-prem later.
00:50 Maya: Great. Can you describe your current stack? Aaron, maybe you can speak to how you're calling models today.
00:56 Aaron: Right now it's a mix — we run smaller NLU models in-house on k8s, vector dbs are in GCS, and we have a prototype calling another vendor's hosted endpoint for summarization. Latency has been okay for internal tooling but customer facing APIs need <200ms p50. We also want predictable unit cost.
01:20 Owen: Good, predictable p50 200ms is tight for hosted depending on model size and sequence length. For hosted we surface performance profiles per model; smaller context models typically hit that easily. For larger models we recommend dedicated reserved capacity or quantized variants.
01:40 Lina: When you say "performance profiles" — is that in the console? We saw reference numbers in a doc but not the console yet.
01:48 Maya: Yes, model catalog in the Console has per-model latency and cost estimates. We'll share a short link to a PDF and the console demo.
01:55 Aaron: On security, we need SOC2 Type II, SSO (SAML), and for private datasets we'd like to use our KMS and audit logs. How does Redwood handle keys and auditability?
02:12 Owen: For hosted we are SOC2 and provide tenant-level audit logs and SSO. For VPC/private you can bring your own KMS via HSM integrations and we enable customer-managed keys for model logs. Note: some telemetry is still required for service health but we can scope retention.
02:32 Priya: Do you have a short checklist for what network ports or IP allowlists we'll need? Our security team will want to onboard them.
02:40 Maya: Absolutely — we'll send the network runbook. For quickstarts, most customers start with API keys and no special networking. If you move to VPC we'll provide CIDR ranges and peering steps.
02:52 Aaron: Regarding credits: what's the typical PLG credit package? We want 30 days to try real traffic.
02:59 Maya: We can issue a 30-day credits bundle sized to roughly 500k tokens of high-usage testing, or pick a custom amount. That'll let you prototype and run baseline tests without billing friction.
03:12 Lina: That sounds good. We want to run a synthetic scenario that mimics our peak bursts — can you help with load testing?
03:19 Owen: Yes, we can run a baseline throughput test with your prompt set, measure p50/p90, and recommend batching/caching and model choices. We'll need your representative prompt set — ideally 50-100 samples covering short and long contexts.
03:32 Aaron: I'll put together prompts — we have both retrieval-augmented generation flows and short Q/A.
03:38 Maya: Perfect. For the hosted quickstart path the usual playbook is: sign up with PLG credits, integrate with API key and SDK (we'll share examples), run simple calls to confirm tokenization and costs, then a Redwood SE-run baseline test, then a two-week pilot.
03:56 Priya: How fast can we get to first token — I mean from sign-up to an authenticated api call? In practice.
04:03 Owen: Most teams hit first token in under an hour if they're using a Postman or curl example and have their app ready. From zero to integrated in 1–2 business days for a minimal prototype. If you need VPC or SSO that adds time — usually a week to provision and test SSO, and 2–4 weeks for Private on-prem engagements.
04:25 Lina: If we do a hosted pilot and see latency >200ms, what's the escalation? Do you do model fallbacks automatically?
04:33 Owen: We have routing policies — you can configure fallbacks to a smaller/quantized model or to a dedicated pool. For customers on Dedicated we can reserve GPUs to meet latency. For hosted we'll propose model variants and batching tweaks first — often cheaper than jumping to dedicated.
04:49 Aaron: Any good rules of thumb for cost vs latency tradeoffs? We want to avoid overpaying for low-latency when we don't need it.
04:56 Owen: Sure — short: if p50 under SLO possible with batching and prefix KV caching, stay hosted. If you need strict <100ms p50 at peak, Dedicated is usually better since you get reserved capacity. Also quantization (8-bit) can reduce cost by 30–60% depending on model with modest quality tradeoffs. We'll provide quality regression results tied to your eval prompts.
05:20 Maya: One more practical: onboarding SDKs — do you prefer Python or Node?
05:24 Aaron: Python first, Node later.
05:26 Owen: We'll share our quickstart repo and a Python snippet that plugs into your stack. It has key rotation examples and streaming.
05:35 Speaker 1: Quick question — what about rate limits for PLG credits? We might spike during tests.
05:40 Maya: PLG accounts have default rate limits but we can temporarily raise them for benchmark windows. We'll coordinate with you.
05:47 Lina: Great. Any legal or procurement blockers we should be aware of before pilot?
05:52 Maya: For hosted pilots, standard terms apply. If you need DPA or data residency clauses, we can pre-share our legal pack. For Private deployments, procurement talks are typically 4–8 weeks.
06:05 Aaron: Sounds fine. Can we get a demo of the Console? Even a quick tour of model catalog, billing, and observability?
06:12 Maya: Sure, Owen can screen share after this but we'll also send a short recorded tour.
06:18 Owen: Quick note — observability exposes per-route token counts, latency histograms, and cost breakdown by prompt. That helps tune batching and model selection.
06:28 Priya: If we move to Dedicated, how does autoscaling work? We have variable traffic and don't want to pay for idle GPUs.
06:36 Owen: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling and burst capacity. You reserve a baseline and configure burst to handle spikes; billing reflects reserved vs burst usage. We also have recommended autoscale policies to hit your SLOs while minimizing idle spend.
06:50 Lina: Okay, let's recap next steps then.
06:53 Maya: Recap: Redwood to send PLG credit link and onboard instructions, Owen to share benchmark spreadsheet and quickstart repo, Olivegrove to provide 50–100 prompt samples and acceptance criteria. Start a 2-week hosted pilot once credits applied.
07:08 Aaron: We'll aim to share prompts by Tuesday and Lina will confirm success metrics.
07:12 Priya: I'll pull network folks in if we need allowlist details.
07:15 Maya: Perfect. Any final questions?
07:18 Lina: No, this is helpful. Thanks.
07:20 Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the baseline test.
07:25 (call ends)
